steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a computer vision paper on improving CLIP zero-shot image classification by having the model infer contextual attributes (like background or orientation) and then condition on them, inspired by human visual perception. Explain what CLIP enables, what is wrong with current prompting, the human-perception motivation, and list our contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- CLIP and zero-shot classification: what it is and why it matters
- Problems with current zero-shot methods / prompts
- Inspiration from human visual perception
- Our method \mathtt{PerceptionCLIP} and list of contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- CLIP
  - Contrastive Language-Image Pretraining; foundational Vision-Language Model (VLM), connects vision and natural language
  - pretrained on 400 million image-caption pairs; associates visual concepts with natural language descriptions
  - foundation for other VLMs, diffusion models, semantic segmentation models
  - key for zero-shot classification: open-ended classification via natural language, no training
  - helps tasks with little/no downstream data: deployment in the wild, medical image classification, satellite object recognition
- Problems with current methods
  - classification treated as text retrieval; no systematic look at text prompts
  - -> sub-optimal generalization, reliance on spurious features, biased predictions, lack of interpretability
  - basic template "a photo of a { class name }" -- much less informative than pretraining captions (Table 9)
  - prompt ensembling: 80 crafted templates; unclear if optimal or why they work
  - class-name retrieval wastes CLIP's ability to understand class-specific features and class-independent attributes (background, orientation) = contextual attributes
- Human visual perception
  - classic neuroscience: three-tiered, context-dependent process (Appendix C)
  - basic attributes (color, orientation) -> scene layout, foreground vs background -> recognizing objects
  - humans unconsciously pick up background, orientation; upside-down image (Figure 1 left): infer rotation, then calibrate classification
  - existing methods overlook contextual attributes
- \mathtt{PerceptionCLIP}
  - zero-shot method emulating inferring and conditioning on contextual attributes
  - better generalization, less reliance on spurious features, better group robustness, interpretability
  - (1) CLIP-understandable prompts with contextual attributes; attribute-aware CLIP score approximating conditional probabilities
  - (2) two proof-of-concept investigations: conditioning on ground-truth attributes helps zero-shot classification and reduces spurious reliance; CLIP can infer attributes itself
  - (3) method (Figure 1): infer contextual attributes, then infer class conditioned on them via descriptions in prompt; like chain-of-thoughts
  - (4) experiments: beats simple templates and prompt ensembles on 11 datasets; near 5\% gain on EuroSAT; worst-group gap reduced by 19\% on Waterbirds and 7\% on CelebA with ViT-L/14

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
CLIP (Contrastive Language-Image Pretraining) is a foundational Vision-Language Model (VLM) that connects vision and natural language. CLIP is pretrained on 400 million image-caption pairs, so it can associate many visual concepts with their natural language descriptions, and this has made it the foundation for many other vision-language models, diffusion models, and semantic segmentation models. This understanding ability of CLIP is important for zero-shot classification, because it allows open-ended image classification through natural language without training. It also helps with many hard tasks where there is little or no downstream data, such as model deployment in the wild, medical image classification and satellite object recognition.

CLIP has strong potential in zero-shot classification, but current methods treat image classification as a text retrieval task and do not systematically look at the text prompts that are used. This leads to sub-optimal generalization, reliance on spurious features, biased predictions, and lack of interpretability. For example, the original CLIP work uses a basic template " a photo of a { class name }" to find the most relevant class for an image, and this is much less informative than the image captions used in pretraining (see examples in Table 9). Another method, prompt ensembling, uses 80 crafted templates to get better generalization. But it is still not clear if these templates are optimal and why they work. Because these methods treat zero-shot classification as just a class name retrieval problem, they may waste CLIP's ability to understand both class-specific features and class-independent attributes like background and orientation (we call these contextual attributes in this paper).

CLIP has unprecedented human-like vision and language understanding, so a natural idea is to take inspiration from human visual perception. Classic neuroscience describes human visual perception as a three-tiered, context-dependent process: first seeing basic visual attributes like color and orientation, then analyzing the scene layout and separating foreground from background, and finally recognizing objects (see details in Appendix C). For example, when humans classify objects in images, we unconsciously pick up contextual attributes like the background and orientation, and with an upside-down image (Figure 1 left), we first infer that the image is rotated and then adjust our classification accordingly. This hierarchical and context-dependent process is different from existing classification methods, which ignore contextual attributes.

- \mathtt{PerceptionCLIP}: emulate inferring and conditioning on contextual attributes -> generalization, less spurious reliance, group robustness, interpretability
- Contributions
  - (1) CLIP-understandable prompts with contextual attributes; attribute-aware CLIP score for conditional probabilities
  - (2) two proof-of-concept investigations: ground-truth attributes help, reduce spurious reliance; CLIP can infer attributes itself
  - (3) the method (Figure 1): infer attributes, then class conditioned on them in the prompt; like chain-of-thoughts
  - (4) results: 11 datasets vs simple templates and prompt ensembles; near 5\% on EuroSAT; gap reduced 19\% Waterbirds, 7\% CelebA, ViT-L/14

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
CLIP (Contrastive Language-Image Pretraining) is a foundational Vision-Language Model (VLM) that connects vision and natural language. CLIP is pretrained on 400 million image-caption pairs, so it can associate many visual concepts with their natural language descriptions, and this has made it the foundation for many other vision-language models, diffusion models, and semantic segmentation models. This understanding ability of CLIP is important for zero-shot classification, because it allows open-ended image classification through natural language without training. It also helps with many hard tasks where there is little or no downstream data, such as model deployment in the wild, medical image classification and satellite object recognition.

CLIP has strong potential in zero-shot classification, but current methods treat image classification as a text retrieval task and do not systematically look at the text prompts that are used. This leads to sub-optimal generalization, reliance on spurious features, biased predictions, and lack of interpretability. For example, the original CLIP work uses a basic template " a photo of a { class name }" to find the most relevant class for an image, and this is much less informative than the image captions used in pretraining (see examples in Table 9). Another method, prompt ensembling, uses 80 crafted templates to get better generalization. But it is still not clear if these templates are optimal and why they work. Because these methods treat zero-shot classification as just a class name retrieval problem, they may waste CLIP's ability to understand both class-specific features and class-independent attributes like background and orientation (we call these contextual attributes in this paper).

CLIP has unprecedented human-like vision and language understanding, so a natural idea is to take inspiration from human visual perception. Classic neuroscience describes human visual perception as a three-tiered, context-dependent process: first seeing basic visual attributes like color and orientation, then analyzing the scene layout and separating foreground from background, and finally recognizing objects (see details in Appendix C). For example, when humans classify objects in images, we unconsciously pick up contextual attributes like the background and orientation, and with an upside-down image (Figure 1 left), we first infer that the image is rotated and then adjust our classification accordingly. This hierarchical and context-dependent process is different from existing classification methods, which ignore contextual attributes.

Based on this insight, we propose a zero-shot classification method called \mathtt{PerceptionCLIP}. It emulates an important part of human visual perception, namely inferring and conditioning on the contextual attributes, and this gives improved generalization, less reliance on spurious features, better group robustness, and interpretability. Our contributions are:

(1) We prepare CLIP for perception by building CLIP-understandable text prompts with contextual attributes and by introducing an attribute-aware CLIP score that approximates the conditional probabilities needed for emulating perception.

(2) With two proof-of-concept investigations, we show that conditioning on ground-truth contextual attributes improves CLIP's zero-shot classification and reduces reliance on spurious features. Also, CLIP is able to infer contextual attributes by itself.

(3) Based on these observations we propose \mathtt{PerceptionCLIP}. Given an image, as shown in Figure 1, it first uses CLIP to infer contextual attributes. Then it uses CLIP to infer the class conditioned on the attributes, by putting the descriptions of the inferred attributes into the prompt. This two-step inference is similar to the concept of chain-of-thoughts in language models.

(4) We show empirically that \mathtt{PerceptionCLIP} does well in both standard generalization and group robustness, and it has improved interpretability. For generalization, it consistently beats baselines that use simple templates and prompt ensembles on 11 datasets. For example, it gives a near 5\% accuracy gain on the EuroSAT dataset. For group robustness, it reduces the gap between average accuracy and worst group accuracy by 19\% on the Waterbirds dataset and 7\% on the CelebA dataset with ViT-L/14, so it relies less on spurious features.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
CLIP (Contrastive Language-Image Pretraining by [1]) is a foundational Vision-Language Model (VLM) that connects the fields of vision and natural language. By pretraining on 400 million image-caption pairs, CLIP can associate various visual concepts with their corresponding natural language descriptions, which makes it the foundation for numerous other vision-language models [2,3,4,5], diffusion models [6,7], and semantic segmentation models [8]. This understanding capability of CLIP is significant for zero-shot classification [9], enabling open-ended image classification via natural language without training. This capability also addresses many challenging tasks with limited or no downstream data, such as model deployment in the wild [10], medical image classification [11] and satellite object recognition [12].

Although CLIP shows strong potential in zero-shot classification, current methods treat image classification as a text retrieval task and lack a systematic investigation into the text prompts used. This leads to sub-optimal generalization [1], reliance on spurious features [13], biased predictions [14,15], and lack of interpretability [16,17]. For example, [1] uses a basic template " a photo of a { class name }" to identify the most relevant class for an image, which is much less informative than the image captions used during pretraining (see examples in Table 9). Another method, prompt ensembling [1], employs 80 crafted templates for better generalization. Nevertheless, it remains unclear whether these templates are optimal and why they are effective. By treating zero-shot classification simply as a class name retrieval problem, these methods potentially waste CLIP's capability to understand both class-specific features and class-independent attributes such as background and orientation (referred to as contextual attributes in this paper).

Given CLIP's unprecedented human-like vision and language understanding, a natural idea is to draw inspiration from human visual perception. Classic neuroscience [18] describes human visual perception as a three-tiered, context-dependent process: first discerning basic visual attributes like color and orientation, then analyzing scene layout and distinguishing foreground from background, and finally recognizing objects (see details in Appendix C). For example, when humans classify objects in images, we unconsciously acquire contextual attributes like the background and orientation, and in the case of an upside-down image (Figure 1 left), we first infer that the image is rotated and then calibrate our classification accordingly. This hierarchical and context-dependent process contrasts with existing classification methods, which overlook contextual attributes.

Building on this insight, we propose a zero-shot classification method called \mathtt{PerceptionCLIP}, which emulates a crucial part of human visual perception — inferring and conditioning on the contextual attributes — resulting in improved generalization, reduced reliance on spurious features, better group robustness, and interpretability. Our contributions are as follows:

- \rhd (1) We prepare CLIP for perception by structuring CLIP-understandable text prompts with contextual attributes and introducing an attribute-aware CLIP score to approximate the conditional probabilities essential for perception emulation.

- \rhd (2) Through two proof-of-concept investigations, we show that conditioning on ground-truth contextual attributes improves CLIP's zero-shot classification and mitigates reliance on spurious features. Moreover, CLIP is able to infer contextual attributes by itself.

- \rhd (3) Based on these observations, we propose \mathtt{PerceptionCLIP}. Given an image, as shown in Figure 1, it first employs CLIP to infer contextual attributes. Then, it uses CLIP to infer the class conditioned on the attributes by incorporating the descriptions of the inferred attributes into the prompt. This two-step inference resembles the concept of chain-of-thoughts in language models.

- \rhd (4) We empirically demonstrate that \mathtt{PerceptionCLIP} excels in both standard generalization and group robustness, with improved interpretability. For generalization, it consistently outperforms baselines that use simple templates and prompt ensembles on 11 datasets. For example, it provides a near 5\% accuracy gain on the EuroSAT dataset. For group robustness, it reduces the gap between average accuracy and worst group accuracy by 19\% on the Waterbirds dataset and 7\% on the CelebA dataset with ViT-L/14, showing less reliance on spurious features.
